explanations: Oral potassium is suitable for many mild or moderate cases, but K 2.1 mmol/L with ventricular ectopy is high-risk and needs monitored rapid correction. Severe magnesium deficiency also requires treatment.
IV potassium is needed, but magnesium 0.42 mmol/L can perpetuate renal potassium wasting and arrhythmias. Both should be replaced with close biochemical and ECG monitoring.

Correct: life-threatening hypokalaemia with ECG changes requires carefully controlled parenteral correction. Clinical distinction: Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia refractory until both are corrected.

Magnesium correction is important, but withholding potassium in severe symptomatic hypokalaemia leaves immediate electrical instability untreated. Replace both using appropriate safe infusion protocols.

Changing chronic diuretic treatment may prevent recurrence but cannot address acute ventricular ectopy and marked electrolyte depletion. The immediate priority is controlled IV replacement and monitoring.
pearl: Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia refractory until both are corrected.
pivot: Mild asymptomatic hypokalaemia can often be treated orally and medication-adjusted.

steps: Give controlled IV KCl and MgSO4 replacement with continuous ECG/electrolyte monitoring.
Monitored diluted IV KCl at protocol-approved rate/concentration and correct Mg.
Frequent serum K/Mg and ECG, adjust for renal function.
Modify causative medications and arrange follow-up electrolyte checks.
management.safety: Never administer IV potassium as undiluted push.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 35-year-old with daily heroin use has relapsed multiple times after short detoxification programmes and suffered one nonfatal overdose. He asks for 'something that stops cravings' and wants to continue working. He is not intoxicated and has capacity.
ask: Which strategy has the strongest evidence for reducing overdose and improving retention?
options: Offer a further short inpatient detoxification programme without maintenance.
Start extended-release naltrexone immediately while current opioid use continues.
Provide overdose education and take-home naloxone as the only intervention.
Offer maintenance methadone or buprenorphine with psychosocial support.
Use scheduled supervised withdrawal each month rather than ongoing treatment.
explanations: Detoxification may be part of an individual care plan, but repeated withdrawal without maintenance has high relapse and overdose risk. Opioid agonist treatment improves retention and reduces mortality.

Naltrexone is an option for selected patients after full detoxification; starting it while physically opioid dependent may precipitate withdrawal. It does not have the same broad retention evidence as methadone/buprenorphine in this repeated-relapse scenario.
Take-home naloxone is important harm reduction, especially after an overdose, but it does not treat dependence or cravings. Combine overdose prevention with evidence-based maintenance treatment.

Correct: opioid agonist maintenance lowers mortality and improves retention compared with repeated detox alone. Clinical distinction: Evidence-based OUD care includes agonist maintenance, harm reduction, naloxone, infection care and psychological support.

Scheduled withdrawal alone does not provide sustained protection from cravings and overdose for someone repeatedly relapsing after detoxification. Ongoing opioid agonist maintenance is more effective at retention and harm reduction.
pearl: Evidence-based OUD care includes agonist maintenance, harm reduction, naloxone, infection care and psychological support.
pivot: Some patients prefer antagonist therapy after full detox, but it requires careful induction and engagement.

steps: Offer maintenance methadone or buprenorphine with psychosocial support.
Offer buprenorphine or methadone via accredited service with correct induction and titration.
Take-home naloxone, safer-use education, hepatitis/HIV testing and vaccination.
Peer support, counselling, social needs, long-term follow-up.
management.safety: Buprenorphine started before adequate withdrawal can precipitate withdrawal; specialist induction pathways matter.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 67-year-old with severe hypertension develops sudden dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. BP 206/112 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 80% despite nasal oxygen, diffuse crackles and marked distress. He remains conscious and cooperative.
ask: Which immediate strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV furosemide first, assessing respiratory support after diuresis begins.
Initiate NIV and titrated IV nitrate infusion while continuing acute pulmonary oedema support.
Use high-flow oxygen alone and await a bedside echo before vasodilation.
Start IV beta blockade to lower BP before addressing respiratory distress.
Give a crystalloid challenge before nitrates because tachycardia implies hypovolaemia.
explanations: IV diuretics can help volume overload, but hypertensive flash pulmonary oedema with marked hypoxaemia needs immediate respiratory support. Non-invasive ventilation and vasodilators can rapidly reduce work of breathing and pulmonary congestion.

Correct: hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary oedema needs rapid oxygenation/ventilatory support and afterload reduction. Clinical distinction: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, NIV plus rapidly acting vasodilators may relieve distress quickly while diuresis removes excess fluid.
Oxygen is essential, but profound hypoxaemia and distress despite standard oxygen favour early positive-pressure support. Echo is useful after stabilisation but should not delay treatment.

Reducing cardiac workload matters, but IV beta blockade is not the immediate strategy during acute decompensated pulmonary oedema and may worsen pump failure. Controlled vasodilation and NIV are more appropriate with severe hypertension.
Pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles and severe hypertension indicate hydrostatic lung oedema, not hypovolaemia. Large fluid loading would aggravate pulmonary congestion.
pearl: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, NIV plus rapidly acting vasodilators may relieve distress quickly while diuresis removes excess fluid.
pivot: If severely hypotensive with cool peripheries, avoid nitrates and manage potential cardiogenic shock with critical-care input.

steps: Initiate NIV and titrated IV nitrate infusion while continuing acute pulmonary oedema support.
Titrated nitrates if BP supports it and IV loop diuretic where overloaded; avoid routine opioids.
ECG/troponin, arrhythmia, BP, chest imaging, renal function and echo; reassess cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic cause.
Frequent SpO2, RR, consciousness, BP and urine output.
management.safety: NIV requires monitoring and cooperation; altered consciousness, inability to protect airway or worsening shock may mandate intubation.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 33-year-old at 31 weeks presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She has no contractions, BP 120/76 mmHg and fetal heart rate is reassuring. A scan at 20 weeks showed a low-lying anterior placenta.
ask: Which immediate assessment is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform speculum assessment before ultrasound to locate the cervix and bleeding.
Perform maternal–fetal assessment and ultrasound before vaginal examination.
Use digital cervical examination immediately to determine labour progression.
Observe on the ward without imaging because maternal and fetal vitals are normal.
Give tocolysis to prevent contractions before identifying the bleeding source.
explanations: A gentle speculum exam may be appropriate once clinically safe, but placental position should be established by ultrasound before potentially hazardous vaginal examinations in suspected placenta praevia. Maternal and fetal stability remain the first assessment priorities.

Correct: suspected placenta praevia requires safe evaluation without digital vaginal exam. Clinical distinction: Painless antepartum bleeding with prior low placenta suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise: NO digital vaginal exam.
A digital vaginal examination can disrupt a placenta covering or near the internal os and cause severe haemorrhage. It should be avoided until previa is excluded by imaging.

Stable observations do not make third-trimester bleeding benign. Assessment should include maternal haemodynamics, fetal status and placental localisation, with readiness to escalate if bleeding increases.
Without contractions, tocolysis does not address the cause and can mask or delay necessary assessment. Confirm placental location and fetal well-being first.
pearl: Painless antepartum bleeding with prior low placenta suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise: NO digital vaginal exam.
pivot: Painful bleeding with a tender hypertonic uterus suggests placental abruption, which may have concealed blood loss.

steps: Perform maternal–fetal assessment and ultrasound before vaginal examination.
Transabdominal and/or transvaginal ultrasound safely determines placental relation to cervix.
Senior obstetric review; anti-D when indicated, antenatal steroids if preterm birth risk and timing/location of delivery based on ongoing bleeding.
management.safety: Never perform digital vaginal exam in suspected placenta praevia before imaging.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 49-year-old with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis has persistent abdominal pain and raised inflammatory markers on day 4. CT shows pancreatic necrosis but no gas in collections. She is afebrile, haemodynamically stable and has no cultures suggesting infection.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Start antibiotics because the presence of any pancreatic necrosis implies infection.
Keep her nil by mouth until necrosis resolves on CT imaging.
Arrange early endoscopic drainage of all necrotic collections on day four.
Begin prophylactic antifungal therapy because high CRP predicts fungal necrosis.
Provide supportive pancreatitis care without prophylactic antibiotics.
explanations: Pancreatic necrosis may be sterile. Antibiotics are appropriate for confirmed or strongly suspected infection or another source, not solely for a CT appearance without fever, gas or sepsis.
Early enteral nutrition is generally preferred when feasible in acute pancreatitis. Prolonged bowel rest is not routine therapy for stable sterile necrosis and may worsen nutritional outcomes.

Intervention is reserved for infected or symptomatic collections under appropriate timing and expertise, usually deferred until maturation when possible. Day-four stable sterile necrosis does not warrant routine drainage.
Inflammation and raised CRP alone do not prove fungal infection or justify antifungal prophylaxis. Monitor for clinical deterioration and treat a demonstrated infection.

Correct: sterile necrosis needs organ support and monitoring, not routine antimicrobial treatment. Clinical distinction: Pancreatic necrosis can be sterile. Treat infected necrosis with antibiotics and appropriately timed drainage/source control, but do not prophylax sterile tissue.
pearl: Pancreatic necrosis can be sterile. Treat infected necrosis with antibiotics and appropriately timed drainage/source control, but do not prophylax sterile tissue.
pivot: If gas, bacteraemia, sepsis or clinical deterioration suggests infected necrosis, start targeted antibiotics and discuss step-up drainage.

steps: Provide supportive pancreatitis care without prophylactic antibiotics.
Judicious fluids, adequate analgesia, early oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated and thromboprophylaxis when safe.
Look for fever, gas in collection, bacteraemia or new organ dysfunction; delay invasive intervention for sterile stable necrosis.
Multidisciplinary step-up drainage/necrosectomy for infected or symptomatic collections.
management.safety: Routine prophylactic carbapenems and early necrosectomy are not indicated in stable sterile necrosis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 27-year-old reports sudden distressing images of harming her baby, which she finds abhorrent and inconsistent with her beliefs. She avoids knives and repeatedly seeks reassurance. She has never wanted to harm the infant, recognises thoughts are her own and has no hallucinations or fixed delusions.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Admit for assessment of postpartum psychosis before attempting OCD-focused care.
Use close infant supervision as the sole intervention until thoughts stop.
Offer reassurance and psychoeducation without formal risk or mental-state review.
Offer exposure and response prevention CBT; consider an SSRI if needed.
Treat with an antipsychotic first because the content involves infant harm.
explanations: Urgent assessment is warranted if psychotic features or intent emerge, but ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with intact insight and avoidance are more suggestive of perinatal OCD. Automatic psychosis labelling may increase distress and stigma.

Supportive supervision can form part of a safety plan when indicated, but does not treat the obsession-compulsion cycle. An individualised risk evaluation followed by evidence-based therapy is needed.

Compassionate explanation that intrusive thoughts can be ego-dystonic is helpful, yet assessment remains essential, and persistent significant distress warrants structured treatment rather than reassurance alone.

Correct: harm obsessions respond to ERP and serotonergic treatment, with proportionate risk assessment. Clinical distinction: Unwanted ego-dystonic harm thoughts with reassurance seeking and avoidance suggest OCD; command hallucinations or delusional intent change urgency.

Antipsychotics are not first-line for OCD solely because the images are violent. The patient recognises them as unwanted and implausible; ERP-based CBT, with an SSRI when appropriate, targets the mechanism.
pearl: Unwanted ego-dystonic harm thoughts with reassurance seeking and avoidance suggest OCD; command hallucinations or delusional intent change urgency.
pivot: If the patient believes an external voice commands harming the infant or acts on the belief, consider psychotic disorder/postpartum psychosis and safeguarding.

steps: Offer exposure and response prevention CBT; consider an SSRI if needed.
Offer structured CBT with ERP; consider SSRI when indicated, including perinatal risk–benefit discussion.
Address avoidance, sleep, family reassurance cycles and monitor functioning and symptom severity.
management.safety: Avoid assuming all intrusive harm obsessions indicate dangerousness, but do not omit infant safety assessment.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 33-year-old receives a high-voltage electrical shock at work and falls. There are small entry and exit burns, severe forearm pain and swelling, dark urine and ECG shows frequent ventricular ectopy. BP is currently 110/68 mmHg.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management bundle?
options: Monitor ECG continuously and assess occult trauma, myoglobinuria and compartment pressure.
Give IV fluids and urine monitoring but defer ECG telemetry if BP remains normal.
Treat the entry burns and delay limb assessment until creatine kinase returns.
Focus on arrhythmia monitoring and defer a trauma survey without visible fractures.
Perform immediate fasciotomy in all high-voltage shocks despite no pressure assessment.
explanations: Correct: hidden electrical tissue injury and arrhythmia risk mandate inpatient care. Clinical distinction: High-voltage injury is about current path and deep damage, not surface burn area.
Rhabdomyolysis care includes appropriate IV fluids and renal/electrolyte monitoring, but documented ventricular ectopy makes ECG monitoring essential even when BP is initially normal.
Small cutaneous burns can conceal deep muscle injury. Progressive forearm pain and swelling require urgent compartment evaluation, and dark urine suggests myoglobinuria even before CK results.

Arrhythmia monitoring is appropriate, but high-voltage exposure with a fall can produce fractures, occult trauma, deep burns and compartment syndrome. A full trauma and limb assessment cannot be omitted.

Fasciotomy may be urgently required when compartment syndrome is clinically established, but is not performed automatically after every electrical injury. Assess evolving pain, neurovascular function and pressures when indicated.
pearl: High-voltage injury is about current path and deep damage, not surface burn area.
pivot: A low-voltage household exposure with normal ECG, no symptoms and no trauma may be suitable for discharge per local policy.

steps: Monitor ECG continuously and assess occult trauma, myoglobinuria and compartment pressure.
CK, potassium, renal tests, urinalysis and serial limb neurovascular/compartment assessments.
Titrated isotonic fluids for rhabdomyolysis while watching urine output and overload.
Burns, cardiology, orthopaedics/vascular input for significant injury.
management.safety: Hyperkalaemia and compartment syndrome may develop despite reassuring early skin examination.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 32-year-old at 35 weeks with a documented velamentous cord insertion has spontaneous rupture of membranes followed immediately by bright-red bleeding. Maternal BP is normal, but fetal heart rate falls to 60/min and remains there.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Start corticosteroids and observe fetal heart rate for 24 hours if bleeding stops.
Perform a speculum examination to confirm fetal-vessel rupture before theatre.
Proceed to emergency Caesarean for bleeding vasa praevia and fetal compromise.
Apply tocolysis to delay delivery until 37 weeks if maternal BP is stable.
Induce vaginal delivery quickly because maternal haemodynamics are normal.
explanations: Antenatal steroids help preterm lung maturation when delivery can be safely delayed, but sustained fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture and bleeding is an immediate emergency. Waiting exposes the fetus to fatal haemorrhage.
Clinical suspicion is already very high with velamentous vessels, post-ROM bleeding and fetal bradycardia. Speculum examination must not delay emergency delivery.

Correct: fetal vessels can bleed rapidly despite maternal stability and require immediate birth. Clinical distinction: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal bradycardia is vasa praevia until excluded, especially with velamentous insertion.
Fetal compromise in suspected vasa praevia is not amenable to tocolysis. Urgent birth is needed despite maternal stability because the bleeding may be fetal.
Maternal observations may remain normal during massive fetal blood loss. Vaginal induction is too slow with persistent FHR 60/min; emergency Caesarean offers the quickest rescue.
pearl: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal bradycardia is vasa praevia until excluded, especially with velamentous insertion.
pivot: Placenta praevia causes maternal bleeding, whereas vasa praevia rupture may devastate fetus while mother stays stable.

steps: Proceed to emergency Caesarean for bleeding vasa praevia and fetal compromise.
Maternal ABC, IV access, fetal monitoring and rapid theatre transfer.
Neonatal assessment for acute anaemia/hypovolaemia and transfusion if required.
management.safety: Do not wait for maternal shock; the fetus can exsanguinate in minutes.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 7-week-old has frequent paroxysms of cough ending in brief apnoea and cyanosis. Immunisations are not yet complete. An older sibling has a prolonged cough. The infant is afebrile, but SpO2 drops during episodes.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange PCR testing and observe at home because there is no fever.
Give macrolide therapy but defer admission unless pneumonia develops.
Admit for pertussis treatment with macrolide and apnoea monitoring.
Treat presumed bronchiolitis supportively and avoid contact prophylaxis review.
Give the next routine pertussis vaccine dose as the primary acute treatment.
explanations: Young infants with pertussis may be afebrile yet have life-threatening apnoea. Diagnostic samples can be collected promptly, but a suggestive exposure and paroxysmal cough with cyanosis require inpatient evaluation.
A macrolide can reduce transmission and may benefit early disease, but hypoxaemic apnoea episodes in a six-week-old warrant hospital monitoring regardless of fever or radiographic pneumonia.

Correct: a young partially immunised infant with coughing paroxysms, apnoea and household exposure has suspected pertussis. Admit for respiratory monitoring and supportive care, send PCR testing as appropriate, start an age-appropriate macrolide and give infection-control and contact prophylaxis advice.

Bronchiolitis can cause apnoea in small infants, but post-tussive cyanosis, a prolonged cough in a household contact and incomplete immunisation raise pertussis strongly. Isolation and exposure management should be considered.
Vaccination is crucial for future protection and contact strategies, but it is not treatment for an active infant illness. Provide macrolide and monitoring as clinically indicated.
pearl: Pertussis in young infants may cause apnoea rather than a characteristic whoop; protect high-risk household contacts.
pivot: An older immunised child with mild prolonged cough may receive outpatient evaluation depending on severity.

steps: Admit for pertussis treatment with macrolide and apnoea monitoring.
Nasopharyngeal PCR when indicated and macrolide per infant age/local dosing.
Droplet precautions and public-health notification/contact prophylaxis as indicated.
Feeding, hydration and family vaccination/cocooning advice.
management.safety: Do not prescribe unsafe cough suppressants or assume afebrile illness is benign.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

skill: Fat embolism syndrome after long-bone fracture
context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 20-year-old two days after femoral fracture develops acute hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae across the upper chest. CXR shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates and platelet count has fallen. CT pulmonary angiography shows no major thrombus.
ask: Which diagnosis and management are MOST appropriate?
options: Support oxygenation and stabilise fractures in fat embolism syndrome.
Start full-dose anticoagulation for presumed occult thromboembolism.
Give IV antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia as the sole initial response.
Begin diuretics for presumed cardiogenic oedema after long-bone trauma.
Arrange routine systemic thrombolysis for suspected microscopic emboli.
explanations: Correct: respiratory and neurological involvement after long-bone trauma is typical; treatment is supportive. Clinical distinction: FES after long-bone fracture often presents 24–72 hours later with respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae.

Pulmonary embolism is a competing cause of hypoxaemia after trauma, but CTPA shows no major thrombus and the triad of hypoxaemia, neurological changes and petechiae after fracture is typical of fat embolism. Anticoagulation is not specific therapy for FES.

Aspiration or pneumonia can cause diffuse infiltrates and hypoxaemia but do not as readily account for petechiae, thrombocytopenia and neurological findings two days after a femoral fracture. Supportive critical care is the priority.
Fluid overload can contribute to hypoxaemia, but rash and altered mentation with the temporal fracture link support fat embolism; empiric diuresis may worsen haemodynamics without signs of overload.
Systemic thrombolysis targets major thrombotic emboli in selected unstable cases, not microscopic fat emboli. Bleeding risk is especially problematic in the recent-trauma setting.
pearl: FES after long-bone fracture often presents 24–72 hours later with respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae.
pivot: A haemodynamically unstable patient with new right ventricular strain may still need workup for thrombotic PE.

steps: Support oxygenation and stabilise fractures in fat embolism syndrome.
Exclude PE, infection and head injury; monitor ABG, neurological state and platelets.
Prompt fracture immobilisation/fixation when physiologically feasible.
Fluids balanced against ARDS, monitor kidneys and complications.
management.safety: Routine steroids and anticoagulation have no established role solely to treat FES.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 32-year-old presents with gum bleeding, bruising and fatigue. FBC shows Hb 82 g/L, platelets 22 ×10^9/L and abnormal promyelocytes on film. INR 1.7, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L, D-dimer high. Molecular confirmation is pending.
ask: Which intervention is MOST appropriate before molecular confirmation?
options: Give platelet transfusion as the only treatment until bone marrow confirmation.
Begin ATRA now with aggressive coagulopathy correction for presumed promyelocytic leukaemia.
Wait for PML–RARA molecular results before prescribing leukaemia therapy.
Start intensive induction chemotherapy first, adding ATRA only if confirmed.
Give IV heparin routinely to prevent the coagulopathy of acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
explanations: Blood products may be urgently required to correct thrombocytopenia and low fibrinogen, but they do not suppress the underlying promyelocytic leukaemia. ATRA must begin as soon as APL is strongly suspected.

Correct: suspected APL is a haematological emergency with early fatal DIC; ATRA should not wait for PML-RARA confirmation. Clinical distinction: APL is 'treat on suspicion': ATRA can rapidly reduce coagulopathy-driven early deaths.

Waiting for molecular confirmation may lead to catastrophic intracranial or other bleeding from APL-associated DIC. Start ATRA immediately while arranging definitive testing and haematology-directed supportive transfusions.

Definitive induction is specialist-directed and depends on risk and confirmation, but ATRA should not be postponed until chemotherapy starts. Early differentiation therapy is a unique lifesaving priority.
Heparin is not routine first-line treatment for APL coagulopathy in a bleeding-prone patient with low fibrinogen and platelets. Correct coagulopathy aggressively and start disease-directed therapy.
pearl: APL is 'treat on suspicion': ATRA can rapidly reduce coagulopathy-driven early deaths.
pivot: Other AML subtypes need prompt specialist treatment, but APL is uniquely time-critical for empiric ATRA.

steps: Begin ATRA now with aggressive coagulopathy correction for presumed promyelocytic leukaemia.
Start all-trans retinoic acid via haematology and send molecular testing.
Support platelets, fibrinogen and coagulation targets with blood products per APL pathway.
DIC, differentiation syndrome, organ function and infection.
management.safety: Avoid invasive procedures until coagulopathy is controlled.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 47-year-old takes diazepam 25 mg daily for five years. His supply ended four days ago. He now has severe anxiety, tremor, insomnia, sweating and a generalised seizure. Glucose and electrolytes are normal.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give an SSRI now and taper diazepam rapidly without replacement dosing.
Treat the seizure once, then discharge with strict abstinence instructions.
Switch to a short-acting sedative and stop all benzodiazepines the next day.
Give antipsychotic monotherapy to control agitation and prevent further seizures.
Stabilise benzodiazepine withdrawal, then gradually taper under supervision.
explanations: An SSRI may treat an underlying anxiety disorder over time but cannot acutely prevent recurrent benzodiazepine withdrawal seizures. Safe withdrawal usually requires re-stabilisation with an appropriate benzodiazepine and planned taper.

Withdrawal seizures after long-term daily diazepam imply a medically significant withdrawal syndrome requiring observation and management. One acute seizure treatment without stabilisation leaves recurrence risk.

Rapid cessation after long-term benzodiazepine exposure can provoke further seizures and autonomic symptoms. Taper speed should be individualised after stabilising acute withdrawal, often over an extended period.
Antipsychotics do not correct the GABAergic withdrawal mechanism and can lower seizure threshold in some circumstances. They should not replace benzodiazepine-based withdrawal management.

Correct: a withdrawal seizure signals complicated high-risk dependence requiring monitored management. Clinical distinction: Abrupt benzodiazepine cessation can be dangerous after chronic use; slow taper and monitoring are safer.
pearl: Abrupt benzodiazepine cessation can be dangerous after chronic use; slow taper and monitoring are safer.
pivot: Brief low-dose use without dependence may produce rebound insomnia without severe withdrawal.

steps: Stabilise benzodiazepine withdrawal, then gradually taper under supervision.
Supervised benzodiazepine regimen, titrate then gradually taper based on dependence and risk.
Autonomic instability, seizures, delirium, mental state and sedation.
CBT for anxiety/insomnia, non-addictive treatments and coordinated prescriber follow-up.
management.safety: Do not abruptly stop high-dose benzodiazepines in dependent patients.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 78-year-old with diarrhoea for three days has creatinine 250 µmol/L (baseline 95), dry mucosa, BP 92/58 mmHg, and minimal urine output. He takes ramipril and ibuprofen. No crackles, oedema or hydronephrosis. Urine microscopy is bland.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial approach?
options: Start loop diuretics immediately for oliguria before checking perfusion.
Correct dehydration with assessed isotonic fluids and monitor renal response.
Continue ramipril to protect glomerular filtration throughout hypovolaemia.
Order urgent dialysis based solely on the rise in serum creatinine.
Restrict fluid because reduced urine output always signals fluid overload.
explanations: Furosemide may help selected fluid-overloaded patients, but clinical dehydration and hypotension suggest a prerenal process. Diuresis would worsen perfusion; replace volume thoughtfully and stop nephrotoxic triggers.

Correct: history, hypotension and bland urine suggest pre-renal AKI from volume depletion and nephrotoxic medications. Clinical distinction: Pre-renal AKI responds to restoring effective circulating volume; check for obstruction and medication contributors in every AKI.

ACE inhibitors can be kidney-protective long-term, but during acute dehydration they may worsen haemodynamic AKI by lowering efferent arteriolar tone. Temporarily hold ramipril and avoid NSAIDs while restoring perfusion.

Dialysis is indicated for selected refractory complications such as severe hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload, not simply a numerical rise in creatinine. This patient first needs fluid assessment and monitoring.
Oliguria alone does not prove volume excess. Dry mucosa, diarrhoea and low BP without oedema or crackles support intravascular depletion, so restriction would be harmful.
pearl: Pre-renal AKI responds to restoring effective circulating volume; check for obstruction and medication contributors in every AKI.
pivot: If granular casts persist after perfusion restoration, consider evolving acute tubular injury rather than simply giving more fluid.

steps: Correct dehydration with assessed isotonic fluids and monitor renal response.
Carefully titrated isotonic crystalloid with serial reassessment; temporarily pause NSAIDs and relevant BP/diuretic drugs.
Strict fluid balance, repeat creatinine/electrolytes/ECG when needed, ensure urine output recovers.
Nephrology for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload, uraemic complications or persistent AKI.
management.safety: Small aliquots and frequent reassessment are especially important if concomitant heart failure exists.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 at 34+1 weeks reports that her baby has moved much less than usual since last night. She has no pain, fluid leak or bleeding. BP is normal and doppler confirms fetal heartbeat.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next action?
options: Give fetal movement advice and schedule a routine ultrasound next week.
Perform a biophysical profile before checking fetal heart rate tracing.
Arrange delivery immediately without fetal surveillance or obstetric assessment.
Arrange same-day CTG and risk-based ultrasound for reduced fetal movements.
Rely on a reassuring handheld Doppler finding and arrange review if symptoms recur.
explanations: A persistent reduction from the fetus's normal movement pattern at 34 weeks needs same-day assessment, not delayed routine imaging. Counselling alone cannot establish fetal wellbeing.

Ultrasound-based testing can be useful if indicated, but an initial antenatal fetal assessment typically includes prompt CTG, maternal review and risk-stratified ultrasound. Do not delay baseline fetal monitoring.
Delivery may be indicated after abnormal monitoring or significant clinical risk, but it is not automatic after a single report of reduced movements at 34 weeks. Assess fetal status first.

Correct: reduced fetal movement warrants prompt surveillance; a heartbeat alone does not establish fetal wellbeing. Clinical distinction: Maternal perception of reduced movements is clinically important even when Doppler confirms a fetal heart rate.
A Doppler heartbeat confirms only that the fetus is alive at that moment. It does not exclude compromise or assess variability and accelerations, so formal assessment remains necessary.
pearl: Maternal perception of reduced movements is clinically important even when Doppler confirms a fetal heart rate.
pivot: If CTG is abnormal, expedite senior obstetric review, targeted ultrasound and possible birth depending on gestation and findings.

steps: Arrange same-day CTG and risk-based ultrasound for reduced fetal movements.
Ultrasound for growth, fluid and Dopplers when indicated by risk/recurrent RFM or concerning CTG.
Explain that a normal single assessment does not invalidate future concerns; return promptly if movement reduces again.
management.safety: Do not rely on home Dopplers to assess fetal wellbeing.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation and inconsistent anticoagulation develops sudden severe diffuse abdominal pain. HR 116/min and lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Examination shows a soft abdomen with only mild tenderness despite extreme reported pain.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Arrange colonoscopy to exclude intestinal inflammation before assessing vessels.
Begin empirical antibiotics for presumed colitis and review lactate after fluids.
Arrange immediate mesenteric CTA and urgent surgical consultation.
Obtain non-contrast CT abdomen alone because contrast worsens ischaemia.
Treat the episode as biliary colic and reserve vascular imaging for peritonism.
explanations: Endoscopy can evaluate selected colonic disorders but does not diagnose acute arterial mesenteric occlusion reliably and may delay time-critical revascularisation.

Colitis can cause pain and lactate elevation, but pain far out of proportion to examination in a patient with AF strongly suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia. Antibiotics may accompany care, but vascular imaging and surgery are urgent.

Correct: acute mesenteric arterial embolism causes pain out of proportion and requires rapid vascular imaging and source-control planning. Clinical distinction: Pain out of proportion to examination in AF is an acute mesenteric ischaemia alarm; the abdomen can be deceptively benign early.
CTA is the preferred urgent investigation because it identifies occlusion and intestinal viability clues. Avoiding contrast purely for theoretical kidney risk can delay life-saving diagnosis.
Peritonism may arise only after advanced bowel infarction. Early acute mesenteric ischaemia can present with a soft abdomen and excruciating pain; wait neither for rigidity nor for overt shock.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to examination in AF is an acute mesenteric ischaemia alarm; the abdomen can be deceptively benign early.
pivot: Established peritonitis or bowel necrosis requires urgent laparotomy, not just endovascular restoration.

steps: Arrange immediate mesenteric CTA and urgent surgical consultation.
CTA arterial/portal phases despite renal concerns when high suspicion because delay threatens bowel survival.
Urgent anticoagulation when appropriate and specialist endovascular/open embolectomy or revascularisation.
Laparotomy/resection when necrosis or peritonitis; repeat inspection if viability uncertain.
management.safety: An elevated lactate is a late/nonspecific sign; normal lactate does not exclude early mesenteric ischaemia.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 35-year-old is brought to ED after taking an unknown number of amitriptyline tablets. She is confused, hot, tachycardic at 140/min, hypotensive 88/50 mmHg with dry mucosa and urinary retention. ECG shows QRS duration 150 milliseconds.
ask: Which immediate treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV physostigmine to reverse delirium before reviewing the QRS interval.
Give sodium bicarbonate only after a ventricular arrhythmia develops.
Start IV lidocaine to treat the tachycardia before correcting blood pressure.
Give IV sodium bicarbonate for TCA cardiotoxicity under ECG monitoring.
Use activated charcoal as the sole therapy despite hypotension and QRS widening.
explanations: Physostigmine can worsen conduction abnormalities and is hazardous in suspected TCA overdose with a wide QRS. Sodium bicarbonate addresses sodium-channel blockade, while supportive care addresses airway and circulation.
QRS 150 ms and hypotension already signify severe sodium-channel cardiotoxicity and high risk of malignant arrhythmias. Bicarbonate should be given promptly rather than waiting for VF/VT.

Antiarrhythmic selection in TCA toxicity requires specialist input; lidocaine may have a role in refractory ventricular arrhythmias but does not replace first-line sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS and shock.

Correct: TCA sodium-channel blockade manifests with broad QRS and responds to bicarbonate alkalinisation/sodium loading. Clinical distinction: TCA toxicity with wide QRS is sodium-channel blockade: IV sodium bicarbonate is a key antidotal therapy.
Activated charcoal may be considered only under appropriate timing and airway safeguards; it cannot reverse existing cardiotoxicity. Immediate ABCs and IV bicarbonate take priority.
pearl: TCA toxicity with wide QRS is sodium-channel blockade: IV sodium bicarbonate is a key antidotal therapy.
pivot: In isolated anticholinergic delirium without QRS abnormalities and after toxicology assessment, physostigmine may sometimes be considered.

steps: Give IV sodium bicarbonate for TCA cardiotoxicity under ECG monitoring.
IV sodium bicarbonate boluses/infusion guided by QRS, BP and pH per toxicology protocol.
Benzodiazepines for seizures, fluids/vasopressors as needed and monitor arrhythmias.
Repeat ECG/acid-base/electrolytes and psychiatric self-harm assessment once medically safe.
management.safety: Avoid class IA/IC antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and indiscriminate flumazenil in TCA toxicity.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 45-year-old is found intoxicated beside an unlabeled solvent bottle. pH 7.08, anion gap 32 mmol/L, osmolar gap increased, creatinine 260 µmol/L and urine microscopy has calcium oxalate crystals. He has no measured ethanol.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Start high-dose ethanol infusion without toxicology advice and postpone dialysis assessment.
Start IV fomepizole and urgently assess indications for haemodialysis with toxicology.
Give bicarbonate alone because it neutralises ethylene glycol metabolites.
Use haemodialysis alone while delaying antidote therapy until levels return.
Give large IV calcium supplements to remove oxalate from the kidneys.
explanations: Ethanol can inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase where fomepizole is unavailable but requires close specialist-guided monitoring. Empirical unmonitored dosing and delay in evaluating severe acidosis/AKI are unsafe.

Correct: ethylene glycol metabolism produces toxic acids and renal injury; blockade and extracorporeal removal may be required. Clinical distinction: High anion gap acidosis plus osmolar gap and oxalate crystals suggests ethylene glycol, though gaps vary over time.
Bicarbonate may help severe acidosis as an adjunct but does not block conversion of ethylene glycol to glycolate and oxalate. Fomepizole prevents further toxic metabolite generation.

Dialysis may be strongly indicated with severe acidosis and kidney injury, but antidote therapy should start promptly while arranging extracorporeal removal rather than waiting for confirmatory levels.
Calcium oxalate crystal injury does not improve with indiscriminate calcium loading; this may increase deposition risk. Treat the toxic alcohol and its acid-base complications.
pearl: High anion gap acidosis plus osmolar gap and oxalate crystals suggests ethylene glycol, though gaps vary over time.
pivot: Methanol poisoning more often causes visual toxicity; both use alcohol dehydrogenase inhibition and sometimes dialysis.

steps: Start IV fomepizole and urgently assess indications for haemodialysis with toxicology.
Monitor severe acidosis, hypocalcaemia, potassium and renal dysfunction; dialysis for severe toxicity/criteria.
Poison centre and nephrology; do not wait for special toxic alcohol level if clinical suspicion high.
management.safety: Do not treat asymptomatic osmolar gap alone without interpretation; use toxicology expertise.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 24-year-old at 36 weeks collapses with a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. BP is 184/118 mmHg, she had severe headache and visual changes before convulsing, and proteinuria is present. She has no epilepsy history.
ask: Which immediate therapy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give a loading dose of phenytoin and wait for seizure cessation before BP treatment.
Use antihypertensive medication first and defer magnesium until blood pressure normalises.
Prepare Caesarean immediately while withholding maternal airway and seizure care.
Treat convulsions as primary epilepsy until EEG confirms their mechanism.
Resuscitate and give magnesium sulfate plus treatment of severe hypertension.
explanations: Phenytoin is not preferred first-line seizure treatment for eclampsia. Magnesium sulfate is more effective for preventing recurrent eclamptic convulsions, and the severe hypertension also requires treatment.
Urgent BP control is essential but magnesium is needed now for eclamptic seizure treatment and prevention. These actions occur together after airway and circulation assessment.
Delivery is definitive treatment once the patient is stabilised, but an uncontrolled seizure and critical hypertension must be managed before operative delivery planning.
Late-pregnancy seizure with severe hypertension, visual symptoms and proteinuria is eclampsia until proven otherwise. Waiting for EEG would delay time-critical magnesium treatment.

Correct: eclampsia requires immediate ABC, magnesium, antihypertensive and obstetric definitive planning. Clinical distinction: Eclampsia can develop before, during or after delivery; magnesium sulfate is seizure treatment/prophylaxis, not BP medication.
pearl: Eclampsia can develop before, during or after delivery; magnesium sulfate is seizure treatment/prophylaxis, not BP medication.
pivot: In epilepsy without hypertension or pre-eclampsia features, seizure management differs and anticonvulsant history matters.

steps: Resuscitate and give magnesium sulfate plus treatment of severe hypertension.
Give IV/IM magnesium sulfate loading and maintenance per protocol; monitor reflexes, respiration, urine output.
Rapid-acting antihypertensives while evaluating labs for HELLP and organ dysfunction.
Plan prompt birth once stabilised; prepare neonatal services.
management.safety: Calcium gluconate is antidote to severe magnesium toxicity.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 15-month-old with acute gastroenteritis is lethargic, pulse 168/min, CRT 6 seconds, sunken eyes and no wet nappy for 10 hours. BP is 74/38 mmHg. She can only take small sips.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Start oral rehydration solution in small frequent sips before IV access.
Give a rapid hypotonic crystalloid bolus with reassessment in thirty minutes.
Treat with antiemetic first, then reassess circulation after diarrhoea stops.
Give monitored IV/IO isotonic bolus and reassess shock response.
Give a maintenance-only fluid infusion because rapid boluses always cause harm.
explanations: Oral rehydration is excellent in mild-to-moderate dehydration when perfusion is stable. This child has shock signs—lethargy, CRT 6 seconds, hypotension and oliguria—requiring immediate IV/IO resuscitation.
Hypotonic fluid is not the correct initial resuscitation fluid in paediatric shock. Use an isotonic crystalloid bolus with clinical reassessment and monitor electrolytes.
Antiemetics can facilitate oral rehydration later, but do not restore circulation rapidly enough in frank shock. Stabilise airway, breathing and perfusion first.

Correct: treat hypovolaemic shock first, then maintenance and losses. Clinical distinction: Capillary refill, mental state, pulse quality and urine output define dehydration severity beyond the number of stools.

Fluid boluses must be titrated and reassessed to avoid overload, but withholding an initial isotonic bolus in hypovolaemic shock is dangerous. Maintenance fluids alone are inadequate for resuscitation.
pearl: Capillary refill, mental state, pulse quality and urine output define dehydration severity beyond the number of stools.
pivot: In a well-perfused child with mild/moderate dehydration, oral/NG rehydration is usually preferred.

steps: Give monitored IV/IO isotonic bolus and reassess shock response.
Electrolytes, glucose and weight-based maintenance/deficit plan after shock reversal.
Oral/NG rehydration and feeds as tolerated, replace ongoing losses.
Urine output, electrolytes, perfusion and stool warning signs.
management.safety: Avoid treating a septic child as 'dehydration only' without checking for infection and alternate causes.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 37-year-old has just splashed industrial alkali into both eyes. He has severe pain, blepharospasm and blurry vision. Coworkers started rinsing water for two minutes before arrival.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate next action?
options: Give topical anaesthetic and reassess symptoms before further irrigation.
Continue prolonged eye irrigation with lid eversion and serial ocular surface pH checks.
Neutralise alkali with dilute acidic drops to restore physiological pH rapidly.
Arrange orbital CT before continuing irrigation because the vision is blurred.
Use antibiotic ointment and eye shields, reserving irrigation for specialist review.
explanations: Topical anaesthetic may facilitate effective irrigation and lid opening, but it must not delay copious decontamination. Pain improvement does not guarantee that alkali has been removed.

Correct: alkali burns penetrate ocular tissues rapidly. Immediately irrigate with available clean water or saline, evert lids and remove particles, reassess ocular pH repeatedly until stable and arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment. Do not delay irrigation for formal visual acuity testing.
Direct acid–alkali neutralisation can cause heat generation and additional chemical injury. Irrigate generously with suitable fluid and reassess ocular pH until stable near physiological range.
CT is not the urgent first step in a chemical ocular injury. Every minute of ongoing alkali contact increases corneal penetration and damage; continuous irrigation comes first.
Ointments and shields may be considered after appropriate decontamination and examination. They do not remove caustic material and must not replace immediate prolonged irrigation.
pearl: In ocular chemical injury, irrigate first; history and formal visual examination come after decontamination starts.
pivot: A superficial non-chemical corneal abrasion is managed by examination, analgesia and infection precautions, not prolonged pH-guided irrigation.

steps: Continue prolonged eye irrigation with lid eversion and serial ocular surface pH checks.
Use saline/water immediately; monitor pH and continue until normal with time for rebound testing.
Visual acuity and fluorescein staining after initial irrigation, assess limbal ischaemia.
Urgent ophthalmology for topical medications and follow-up.
management.safety: Do not delay washout waiting for a specific irrigating fluid.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

skill: HIV opportunistic infection with low CD4
stem: A 37-year-old living with HIV, off antiretroviral therapy, has three weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough and fever. CD4 is 45 cells/µL, SpO2 87% room air, CXR shows bilateral diffuse interstitial opacities and LDH elevated.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial therapy?
options: Start high-dose co-trimoxazole and assess need for corticosteroids.
Give empirical IV ceftriaxone alone for a typical bacterial lobar pneumonia.
Start fluconazole alone for presumed pulmonary cryptococcosis.
Commence ART as the only immediate therapy for opportunistic pneumonia.
Treat with azithromycin alone for presumed atypical community pneumonia.
explanations: Correct: PCP with moderate/severe hypoxaemia may benefit from corticosteroids and TMP-SMX. Clinical distinction: Pneumocystis pneumonia causes subacute dyspnoea, dry cough and hypoxaemia disproportionate to examination in advanced HIV.

Standard bacterial pneumonia can cause hypoxaemia but tends to be more acute and focal. The subacute dry cough, diffuse interstitial opacities and CD4 45 strongly support PJP, requiring high-dose co-trimoxazole.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis is possible in severe immunosuppression but is not the classic syndrome here, and fluconazole alone would not treat PJP. Test appropriately if competing diagnoses are suspected.
ART should be planned promptly as part of HIV care, but immune restoration is not immediate treatment for life-threatening PJP. Anti-Pneumocystis treatment and oxygenation assessment are urgent.
Macrolide monotherapy is inadequate for suspected PJP and hypoxaemia at 87% room air. Inpatient treatment and consideration of adjunct corticosteroids based on oxygenation are needed.
pearl: Pneumocystis pneumonia causes subacute dyspnoea, dry cough and hypoxaemia disproportionate to examination in advanced HIV.
pivot: If CD4 higher and lobar consolidation with purulent sputum, bacterial CAP becomes more likely.

steps: Start high-dose co-trimoxazole and assess need for corticosteroids.
TMP-SMX appropriate to severity; adjunct steroids when gas-exchange criteria met.
Oxygen, inpatient monitoring and evaluate treatment response.
ID/HIV team to arrange appropriately timed ART initiation and prophylaxis.
management.safety: Sulfonamide reactions and renal/electrolyte effects require close monitoring.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 30-year-old with schizophrenia refuses oral antipsychotic because she has gained weight and experienced akathisia. She explains treatment benefits and relapse risks clearly, proposes alternative medicines and has no current dangerous behaviour. She is not under a treatment order.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Ask family to encourage adherence by administering medication without her knowledge.
Stop discussion after refusal because clinicians may not offer alternatives.
Use involuntary treatment powers solely because she has schizophrenia.
Respect capacity and negotiate alternatives addressing adverse effects.
Insist on the same antipsychotic dose despite severe akathisia and weight gain.
explanations: Covert medication violates autonomy and can destroy trust unless exceptionally authorised under a lawful, ethically reviewed pathway. A capable patient making an informed refusal should be engaged collaboratively.
Respecting refusal does not mean abandoning care. Explore the distressing adverse effects, reasonable alternative antipsychotics, risk management, psychoeducation and follow-up.

A schizophrenia diagnosis does not automatically remove decision-making capacity or meet statutory involuntary-treatment criteria. Capacity is decision-specific, and she demonstrates understanding and reasoning.

Correct: she demonstrates understanding and deliberation and should be offered shared decisions. Clinical distinction: A capable patient can refuse treatment even when clinicians believe another option is better; address the reasons for refusal.
Insisting on an intolerable regimen may worsen adherence and symptoms. A shared plan could consider dose or drug change, akathisia management and metabolic risk after reviewing options.
pearl: A capable patient can refuse treatment even when clinicians believe another option is better; address the reasons for refusal.
pivot: If acute psychosis prevents appreciation of risk and criteria for compulsory care apply, a different legal process may be considered.

steps: Respect capacity and negotiate alternatives addressing adverse effects.
Akathisia, weight and past response; assess relapse indicators and safety.
Switch medication, reduce adverse effects, psychosocial care or agreed monitoring.
The shared plan, consent/refusal and clear follow-up/safety contacts.
management.safety: Involuntary treatment is regulated by jurisdiction-specific mental health law.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 54-year-old with small-cell lung cancer has serum sodium 111 mmol/L and then a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. BP and oxygenation are currently maintained. Recent labs suggest SIADH and glucose is normal.
ask: Which initial treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give a monitored bolus of hypertonic 3% saline for severe hyponatraemia.
Begin isotonic saline at maintenance rate and recheck sodium in six hours.
Restrict fluids and wait for the seizure to stop as sodium rises gradually.
Give tolvaptan immediately because the likely mechanism is SIADH.
Correct sodium rapidly to 140 mmol/L within the first treatment hour.
explanations: Correct: severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs rapid initial small rise to reverse cerebral oedema, then controlled correction. Clinical distinction: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs a controlled initial sodium rise, not normalisation; rapid total correction risks osmotic demyelination.

Isotonic saline may be appropriate in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, but a seizure at Na 111 mmol/L needs urgent hypertonic 3% saline boluses to reverse cerebral oedema. Monitoring avoids overcorrection.
Fluid restriction can help chronic SIADH after stabilisation, but does not act quickly enough for acute seizures from severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.
Vaptans are not the emergency treatment for hyponatraemic seizures and carry overcorrection risks. Controlled hypertonic saline is standard for severe neurological symptoms.

Rapid complete normalisation risks osmotic demyelination, especially if hyponatraemia is chronic. Aim for an initial modest monitored rise sufficient to control severe symptoms, then limit subsequent correction.
pearl: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs a controlled initial sodium rise, not normalisation; rapid total correction risks osmotic demyelination.
pivot: For mild/asymptomatic SIADH, fluid restriction and treatment of the cause may be first-line under monitoring.

steps: Give a monitored bolus of hypertonic 3% saline for severe hyponatraemia.
Give measured 3% saline boluses per local severe symptomatic hyponatraemia guideline, reassess symptoms and sodium after each.
Frequent sodium measurements and urine output checks, consider desmopressin/re-lowering strategy with specialist advice if rapid water diuresis occurs.
Review SIADH triggers and address tumour/medications after stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not aim for rapid normalisation; chronic hyponatraemia has high osmotic demyelination risk with overcorrection.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 5-year-old with no Hib immunisations has high fever, drooling, muffled voice and inspiratory stridor. He sits forward with chin extended and becomes distressed when staff approach. SpO2 is 94% in room air.
ask: What is the BEST immediate management?
options: Keep child calm and call senior airway team for suspected epiglottitis.
Start nebulised adrenaline before involving the anaesthetic or ENT team.
Place the child supine for lateral neck radiography to verify epiglottic swelling.
Inspect the pharynx with a tongue depressor to distinguish tonsillitis.
Give IV antibiotics first and reassess stridor after the initial dose.
explanations: Correct: suspected epiglottitis is a dangerous upper-airway emergency managed with expert help and minimal distress. Clinical distinction: Drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance and muffled voice suggest supraglottitis rather than uncomplicated croup.

Nebulised adrenaline helps croup but is not definitive for suspected epiglottitis with drooling, tripod posture and muffled voice. It should not delay airway specialists and a controlled management plan.
Forcing a distressed child supine or separating them for imaging can provoke complete upper-airway obstruction. Keep them comfortable, minimise procedures and arrange senior airway control.

Oral examination with a tongue depressor can precipitate laryngospasm and obstruction in suspected epiglottitis. Defer provocative examination until airway experts are present in a controlled setting.
Antibiotics are essential after airway safety is assured, but obstruction can occur suddenly before they work. Expert airway assessment is the immediate priority.
pearl: Drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance and muffled voice suggest supraglottitis rather than uncomplicated croup.
pivot: Barking cough with stridor but no drooling/toxic features suggests viral croup where dexamethasone/nebulised adrenaline are useful.

steps: Keep child calm and call senior airway team for suspected epiglottitis.
Anaesthesia, ENT, paediatrics and theatre support; prepare controlled airway securing by experienced clinician.
Once airway safe, blood cultures if feasible and IV antibiotics per local epiglottitis guideline.
High-acuity monitoring for deterioration; evaluate immunisation status once recovered.
management.safety: Avoid attempts at IV access or imaging if they dangerously upset the child before expert airway control.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 67-year-old with left iliac fossa pain and fever has CT-confirmed sigmoid diverticulitis with a 5.2 cm pericolic abscess. She is haemodynamically stable with no diffuse peritonitis, but WCC is 18 × 10^9/L.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Give IV antibiotics alone without considering source control of a 5 cm abscess.
Schedule elective colonoscopy during the acute episode to drain the abscess.
Give IV antibiotics and ask interventional radiology to assess drainage of pericolic abscess.
Proceed directly to Hartmann surgery despite stability and accessible drainage.
Discharge on oral antibiotics with repeat imaging only if symptoms worsen.
explanations: IV antibiotics are needed, but a 5.2 cm abscess often warrants assessment for image-guided percutaneous drainage depending on safe access. Antibiotics alone may fail to control a collection of this size.

Colonoscopy is generally avoided in active complicated diverticulitis because of perforation risk and is not a method for draining the pericolic abscess. Endoscopic evaluation comes later if indicated.

Correct: large accessible abscesses generally benefit from percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics where feasible. Clinical distinction: Size and accessibility of diverticular abscess guide drainage; physiological stability and peritonitis determine surgical urgency.

Emergency resection is reserved for diffuse peritonitis, instability, failure of non-operative management or other complications. A stable patient may be managed with IV antibiotics and percutaneous drainage if feasible.
A large abscess with fever and leukocytosis requires inpatient observation, IV therapy and source-control planning. Discharge with oral treatment alone risks progression.
pearl: Size and accessibility of diverticular abscess guide drainage; physiological stability and peritonitis determine surgical urgency.
pivot: If generalised purulent/faecal peritonitis or shock develops, operative source control becomes urgent.

steps: Give IV antibiotics and ask interventional radiology to assess drainage of pericolic abscess.
IV antibiotics active against enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, surgical team involvement.
IR evaluation for percutaneous drain of larger accessible collection; surgery if not drainable or clinical deterioration.
Tailor antibiotics to culture, repeat imaging for poor response and plan subsequent bowel assessment per local recommendations.
management.safety: Do not perform colonoscopy during the acute perforated/infected phase.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 30-year-old at 17 weeks gestation has eight weeks of pervasive low mood, anhedonia, marked insomnia and poor oral intake. She previously responded well to sertraline but stopped it when pregnant. She denies current suicidal plans but finds working and self-care difficult.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Recommend psychological therapy alone without discussing prior SSRI response.
Resume sertraline automatically without informed discussion or symptom assessment.
Offer routine admission solely because depression occurs during pregnancy.
Offer perinatal mental-health care and discuss treatment risks and benefits.
Wait until after delivery before addressing disabling depressive symptoms.
explanations: Psychological therapy may be effective and is important to discuss, but marked functional impairment and a prior good response to sertraline justify a balanced shared discussion of medication plus supportive treatment.

A prior response supports considering sertraline, but treatment should be individualised after discussing benefits, pregnancy and neonatal risks, patient values and the consequences of untreated depression.

Admission may be indicated with severe risk, psychosis, inability to maintain safety or other concerns, but pregnancy with depression does not automatically require hospitalisation. Individualised risk assessment is essential.

Correct: significant antenatal depression warrants active treatment; both untreated illness and medication risks should be discussed individually. Clinical distinction: Treating antenatal depression is shared decision-making: severity, prior response, maternal safety and fetal exposure all matter.

Untreated significant antenatal depression can impair nutrition, functioning and maternal well-being, with wider pregnancy consequences. Effective care should not be delayed reflexively until postpartum.
pearl: Treating antenatal depression is shared decision-making: severity, prior response, maternal safety and fetal exposure all matter.
pivot: Suicidal intent, psychosis, inability to eat/drink or severe self-neglect require urgent specialist assessment and possible admission.

steps: Offer perinatal mental-health care and discuss treatment risks and benefits.
Offer CBT/interpersonal therapy and consider restarting previously effective SSRI with perinatal psychiatry/obstetric input.
Early follow-up for symptom response, side effects, sleep, nutrition and postpartum relapse risk.
Communicate with GP, obstetrics and mental health services and plan postnatal support.
management.safety: Do not abruptly discontinue effective psychiatric medication in pregnancy without discussing relapse and withdrawal risks.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

skill: Acute blood loss and permissive hypotension
stem: A 26-year-old with penetrating abdominal trauma has BP 78/40 mmHg, HR 142/min and worsening abdominal distension. FAST shows free fluid. There is no suspected head injury, and emergency laparotomy is available.
ask: Which resuscitation strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give repeated large crystalloid boluses until BP is normal, then consider blood.
Start tranexamic acid and delay surgery until a second FAST scan confirms blood.
Use vasopressors alone to restore perfusion before seeking haemorrhage control.
Activate massive transfusion and balanced blood products while arranging operative haemostasis.
Transfer for CT angiography despite haemodynamic instability and a positive FAST.
explanations: Large crystalloid volumes can cause dilutional coagulopathy, hypothermia and worse bleeding. Haemorrhagic shock from penetrating abdominal trauma warrants early balanced blood product resuscitation and rapid operative control.

Tranexamic acid may be considered promptly within relevant trauma protocols, but it does not replace blood product resuscitation and immediate surgical haemostasis; repeat FAST adds little when shock and free fluid are clear.
Pressors may be temporary adjuncts in selected circumstances, but they cannot replace circulating blood or stop ongoing bleeding. Prioritise haemostatic resuscitation and laparotomy.

Correct: penetrating abdominal trauma with hypotension and positive FAST indicates major intra-abdominal bleeding. Activate trauma and massive transfusion pathways, obtain blood products, use haemostatic resuscitation, prevent hypothermia and proceed urgently to operative haemorrhage control. Avoid excessive crystalloid.
CT is useful for stable trauma patients; this patient is in shock with free abdominal fluid and an available operating theatre. Transfer to scanning delays definitive control.
pearl: Shock with positive FAST after trauma is a bleeding problem requiring haemostatic products and definitive control.
pivot: When severe TBI coexists, higher perfusion targets may be necessary rather than permissive hypotension.

steps: Activate massive transfusion and balanced blood products while arranging operative haemostasis.
Warm blood products balanced per local ratio-guided system, calcium/temperature/acid-base monitoring.
Urgent laparotomy or interventional haemostasis per injury and stability.
Monitor coagulopathy, fibrinogen, platelets, temperature and organ perfusion.
management.safety: Avoid delaying source control for imaging in a clearly unstable bleeding abdomen.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 27-year-old at 18 weeks is RhD negative, has no anti-D antibodies on screening, and sustained moderate abdominal trauma from a road collision. Ultrasound shows viable fetus and no obvious placental bleed.
ask: Which preventive intervention should be considered promptly?
options: Obtain Kleihauer testing first and give anti-D only if fetomaternal haemorrhage is proven.
Defer anti-D because ultrasound shows a viable fetus without placental bleeding.
Repeat the maternal antibody screen after six weeks before deciding prophylaxis.
Give anti-D only postpartum if the newborn is found to be RhD positive.
Give anti-D immunoglobulin now and assess fetomaternal haemorrhage.
explanations: Quantification of fetomaternal haemorrhage may guide dosing after significant trauma, but waiting for a positive test should not delay indicated anti-D prophylaxis for an unsensitised RhD-negative pregnant patient.
Ultrasound cannot exclude microscopic fetomaternal haemorrhage after trauma. Normal fetal heartbeat and a reassuring scan do not remove the risk of maternal sensitisation.
A later antibody screen can detect sensitisation after it occurs, not prevent it. Timely anti-D prophylaxis reduces Rh alloimmunisation risk following sensitising events.
Postpartum prophylaxis is a separate issue; antepartum trauma is a potential sensitising event. Prevention should be considered promptly rather than withheld until birth.

Correct: trauma may cause sensitising FMH and prophylaxis protects unsensitised RhD-negative mothers. Clinical distinction: An RhD-negative unsensitised pregnant patient may require anti-D after sensitising events even if bleeding is not obvious.
pearl: An RhD-negative unsensitised pregnant patient may require anti-D after sensitising events even if bleeding is not obvious.
pivot: If she already has established immune anti-D antibodies, prophylactic anti-D is ineffective and fetal alloimmunisation surveillance is required.

steps: Give anti-D immunoglobulin now and assess fetomaternal haemorrhage.
Confirm Rh type and antibody screen; FMH test when gestation/trauma warrants.
Timely anti-D prophylaxis with dose adjusted per local protocol and FMH volume.
Counsel and document sensitising event and routine future prophylaxis.
management.safety: Do not delay trauma resuscitation for anti-D testing.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: An 8-year-old has dozens of brief daily episodes of abrupt staring lasting 8 seconds. She stops talking mid-sentence and resumes immediately without confusion. Provoked hyperventilation triggers a spell; EEG shows 3-Hz generalised spike-and-wave.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate for uncomplicated childhood absence epilepsy?
options: Start sodium valproate because it treats all generalised childhood seizures equally.
Start ethosuximide as first-line therapy for isolated typical childhood absence seizures.
Prescribe carbamazepine because the episodes feature behavioural arrest.
Observe without treatment because immediate recovery excludes seizures.
Give daily benzodiazepines to suppress every brief lapse in attention.
explanations: Valproate treats generalised epilepsies and may be appropriate with multiple seizure types, but ethosuximide is generally preferred for uncomplicated absence-only epilepsy because of efficacy and tolerability considerations.
Correct: typical isolated absence seizures often respond to ethosuximide. Clinical distinction: Typical absence seizures are brief, frequent, no postictal state and 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG.
Carbamazepine is used for focal seizures and can aggravate typical absence epilepsy. The 3-Hz generalised spike-and-wave EEG is classic for childhood absence seizures.
Prompt recovery is characteristic of typical absence seizures, not proof of daydreaming. Frequent daily spells can impair learning and require treatment.
Chronic benzodiazepines create sedation and tolerance concerns and are not first-line maintenance for uncomplicated childhood absence epilepsy. Select a targeted anti-seizure medicine.
pearl: Typical absence seizures are brief, frequent, no postictal state and 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG.
pivot: If generalised tonic–clonic seizures coexist, valproate or other broad-spectrum treatment may be favoured by specialist (with reproductive safety considerations).

steps: Start ethosuximide as first-line therapy for isolated typical childhood absence seizures.
Ethosuximide when absence-only, dose titration and adverse-effect monitoring per neurology.
Water safety, school recognition and seizure first aid.
Document frequency and EEG/clinical response; reassess for other seizure types.
management.safety: Medication choice changes if the child also has convulsive seizures.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: An 8-year-old with sinusitis has swollen erythematous left eyelids, temperature 38.7°C, painful restricted eye movements and slight proptosis. Visual acuity is reduced compared with the other eye.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Treat with oral antibiotics and next-day review for presumed preseptal cellulitis.
Obtain outpatient sinus imaging before commencing any systemic antibiotics.
Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent orbital imaging and specialist review.
Start IV corticosteroids alone to reduce orbital swelling before antibiotics.
Give topical antibiotics and monitor vision without hospital admission.
explanations: Painful restricted eye movements, proptosis and reduced visual acuity indicate postseptal orbital involvement with risk to sight and intracranial spread. Oral outpatient therapy is insufficient.
Urgent orbital imaging is appropriate, but should accompany admission, antibiotics and ENT/ophthalmology review rather than precede all treatment on an outpatient basis.

Correct: orbital cellulitis needs inpatient treatment and assessment for abscess/intracranial spread. Clinical distinction: Painful limited extraocular movement, proptosis or altered vision distinguishes orbital from preseptal cellulitis.
Steroids may sometimes be an adjunct after appropriate antibiotics and expert input, but alone they could worsen untreated infection. Prompt IV antibacterial therapy is central.
Topical drops cannot adequately treat deep orbital infection. Impaired vision and proptosis require urgent imaging and multidisciplinary inpatient treatment.
pearl: Painful limited extraocular movement, proptosis or altered vision distinguishes orbital from preseptal cellulitis.
pivot: Preseptal infection without orbital signs in a well child can sometimes be treated orally with close review.

steps: Admit for IV antibiotics and urgent orbital imaging and specialist review.
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with local sinus/orbital coverage.
CT/MRI of orbits/sinuses as appropriate and urgent ophthalmology/ENT review.
Surgical drainage if abscess, optic compromise or poor response.
management.safety: Monitor for cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial complications.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 40-year-old with AIDS (CD4 28) has two weeks of headache, fever and blurred vision. LP opening pressure is 38 cm H₂O, CSF cryptococcal antigen positive and meningism mild. BP is stable.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Use amphotericin-based antifungal therapy but defer CSF pressure management.
Give IV dexamethasone routinely for raised pressure and postpone serial LP.
Start antiretroviral treatment immediately before induction antifungals.
Treat cryptococcal meningitis and relieve raised CSF pressure with serial LPs.
Give oral fluconazole alone without therapeutic drainage of high CSF pressure.
explanations: Induction antifungal therapy is crucial, but an opening pressure of 38 cm H2O can be life-threatening and requires active therapeutic CSF pressure reduction. Medication alone may not control pressure.
Routine corticosteroids are not recommended for cryptococcal meningitis and do not replace therapeutic lumbar punctures. Manage elevated intracranial pressure using serial CSF drainage when safe.

ART is important, but initiating it too early during cryptococcal meningitis can increase inflammatory complications. Start appropriate induction antifungals and plan ART timing with HIV/infectious-disease specialists.

Correct: cryptococcal meningitis requires appropriate amphotericin-based induction and active pressure management. Clinical distinction: Raised CSF opening pressure is a major cause of cryptococcal morbidity; serial therapeutic LP saves lives.

Fluconazole alone may be insufficient for severe cryptococcal meningitis depending on resource and regimen, and it does not rapidly relieve markedly raised CSF pressure. Use recommended induction therapy and serial therapeutic LPs.
pearl: Raised CSF opening pressure is a major cause of cryptococcal morbidity; serial therapeutic LP saves lives.
pivot: Tuberculous meningitis has a different drug regimen and may include corticosteroid therapy.
